issues.legal_issue: Possession obtained under an executory agreement for sale, while the parties contemplate a later conveyance and the purchaser recognizes the vendor’s title, is not adverse to the vendor.
material_facts: The original owner placed the purchaser in possession under an agreement for sale.
The transaction was found to be an agreement for sale, not an outright oral transfer, and the parties contemplated a formal sale deed.
The purchaser’s possession during this period was in recognition of the original owner’s title.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s possession was permissive or derivative, held on behalf of the owner, and was not adverse.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession must commence wrongfully and continue against the right of another. Possession referable to a lawful title is not adverse; possession under an executory contract, pending the contemplated conveyance, recognizes the vendor’s title. The Court approved Annamalai Chettiar v. Muthiah Chettiar, ILR 1965 Madras 254.

predicates.possession_under_executory_sale_agreemen: A transferor placed a transferee in possession under an agreement that remained executory.
predicates.formal_conveyance_contemplated: The parties contemplated completing the transfer through a later formal conveyance.
predicates.purchaser_recognized_vendor_title: The transferee possessed the property in recognition of the transferor’s ownership.

issues.definition: When possession under an executory sale agreement is accompanied by a contemplated later conveyance and recognition of the transferor’s title, the possession is not adverse.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking recovery of possession on the strength of title may rely on a predecessor’s possession within the applicable limitation period when that possession was held on behalf of the claimant’s predecessor in title.
material_facts: The claimant sued to recover possession on the basis of a sale deed, and the findings supporting the claimant’s title were not challenged.
The claimant’s predecessor in title had been placed in possession under an agreement for sale and held possession on behalf of the owner during a period falling within twelve years before the suit.
The decree for specific performance obtained by the agreement purchaser had not been executed.
issues.conclusion: The predecessor’s possession within the relevant twelve-year period was established, and the claimant was entitled to a decree for possession; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a title-based claim for possession depends on establishing possession within the applicable limitation period. Because possession under the executory agreement was held on behalf of the owner, it could establish the required possession of the claimant’s predecessor in title. The Court relied on and approved Annamalai Chettiar v. Muthiah Chettiar, ILR 1965 Madras 254.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding to recover possession on the basis of title.
predicates.claimant_title_established: The claimant’s title was established and the findings supporting it were not challenged.
predicates.predecessor_possession_within_limitation: A predecessor in title possessed the property within the period relevant to the claimant’s recovery suit.

issues.definition: In a title-based suit for possession, an established claimant who proves a predecessor’s possession within the applicable limitation period is entitled to a possession decree.
